<advisory severity="concern" guidance="weigh, don't blindly obey">
Fix the gate ordering in item 3: AGENTS.md makes OOB/SOL reachability a blocking prerequisite *before* any package transaction or reboot, but your chain runs "SOL-attach through the RAD" after reboot + post-boot verification. Move the SOL proof ahead of the 5.5.2 upload so a failed boot still has a live recovery path. Also state which rad-* hop provides that proof for SITE-S, since flashing INFRA-158 removes its own jump path during the window.
</advisory>

messages.reasoning:
The advisory is correct: AGENTS.md's hard rule — "Out-of-band access is a blocking prerequisite for every gateway upgrade. Before any package transaction or reboot, prove that the site's rad-* gateway can reach the target's management controller and establish a usable serial-over-LAN session" — wait, that rule is about GATEWAY work (package transaction on gateways where the GATEWAY's rad-* is the OOB). Here, the appliance ITSELF (INFRA-158) is the OOB device. The prior convention says: prove the SOL/console path BEFORE the transaction. For RAD firmware work: if the RAD we're flashing is SITE-S's only OOB device and a flash goes bad, having lured yourself into depending on INFRA-217 (dead mid-window) is exactly the failure mode to guard against — demonstrated by the advisory's mental framing: "SOL-attach through the RAD after reboot + post-boot verification" — after reboot is TOO LATE; the proof must run BEFORE the Unit goes down.

But the ground complexity: For the gateway-upgrade convention, the "SOL attach proof" is *to the gateway's iDRAC through its rad*. For the RAD upgrade itself there is a DIFFERENT recovery question: what is the reset/recovery channel for INFRA-158 itself? The appliances are local on site (in a rack); if SITE-S's RAD dies, "SOL" isn't even what consoles it — not the serial console for RAD itself (the RAD owns the site's serial console per-console port manager). Recovery for a dead site RAD = someone physically re-flash/recovers the appliance (Opengear devices have local UART/recovery JTAG or USB/netconsole path? vendor support = "rescue mode" / recovery procedure at the appliance's serial console? + they could be re-flashed at Opengear-recovery stage (Opengear devices support Hold-reset & TFTP rescue via their own bootloader). So the real pre-gate for a RAD window is:

1. Ensure a verified OOB replacement path COMMON window (another path into the site — e.g., the still-alive `INFRA-90`/`INFRA-89`/`INFRA-43` trans to the site's own gateway iDRAC SOL AS the SOL gate) — but the specific NEW risk during a RAD-only window: a dead INFRA-158 removes the SITE-S RAD function and leaves the SITE without a serial-console recovery layer. So the prerequisite "prove that the site's rad-* gateway can reach the target's management controller and establish SOL" WRITES ITSELF as irrelevant here IF the target is the RAD: the true gate is different:
   - Verify there is a **working alternative serial/console entry** if the flashed appliance dies: for sites, the site devices' iDRAC/iLO interfaces (locally reachable via the OTHER rad's console path from SITE-S's perspective? another site's rad? no).

Hmm, that Advisory's specific framing "state which rad-* hop provides that proof for SITE-S, since flashing INFRA-158 removes its own jump path during the window" catches the truth: for OTHER tools (gateway upgrade), the prerequisite chain ends at the site's own rad-<site>. When we flash THAT SAME rad, no fresh public-path proof through ITSELF exists DURING the window. So during the SITE-S window the OOB path for the SITE collapses progressively: we cannot prove "INFRA-217 SOL" through INFRA-217 (self-referential). What CAN be proven in-window:
- The **existing** (pre-window) SOL/console proof for the site's management devices via INFRA-158 executed at the start of the window and preserved as evidence (so that post-RAD-flash, the site's conhold re-proofs become possible again if the appliance recovers well).
- The **flash's own recovery channel**: Opengear appliances have a bootloader "recovery mode" (On Hazumian/Opengear ACM700x: hold down the reset button and TFTP rescue) — PHYSICAL access. Not automatable remotely. So we accept: a failed SITE-S flash may require physical/serial-on-site recovery — the harness number.

So re-ordering the plan per the concern is genuinely useful for RAD-type windows in a DIFFERENT tense than the gateway-update generic rule: "before the transaction, prove every NON-RAD management path that the RAD also carries, and enumerate the sites' secondary recovery channels that will survive a RAD outage" + "record which OTHER rad path (SITE-D's INFRA-90?) can serve as the proof channel during the SITE-S window" — the site-NAT staleness: the SOL attaches happen through each SITE'S OWN rad, not through another. For the SITE-S window, the SOL proof (from an earlier window) already exists for INFRA-4 (done a while ago per this work's procedure during the its "rad proof preconditions" (AGENTS: "Before using an Ansible RAD aggregate operationally, reconcile it to RackTables")). Honest ordering update:

**Modified per-unit sequence:**
1. Public OOB gate (fresh proof workstation → ACTIVE public rad-<site> LTE → its controller → SOL attach for the SITE'S GATEWAY briefly) — done BEFORE the flash window opens: this proves the very OOB we'll depend on post-reboot is alive pre-flash (i.e., it's the WAIT-gate: entry-exit state equality). This ensures we know the BASELINE state (i.e., post-flash recovery checks can assert equality here).
2. (If the target is the rad itself) enumerate in-window fallbacks: the lonely console/serial for this rad; reflash boot via bootloader (documented rec CUSTH-34).
3. Pre-change backup.
4. Flash via browser upload (chosen vehicle).
5. Reboot; convert the post-boot state and require actual == baseline (same interface names, same SIM pair, same tun0 presence).
6. Second public-path proof per step 1's shape (now through the newly-flashed RAD) → this closes the loop: AGENTS rule for the NEXT window (the gateway upgrade) stays satisfied BECAUSE the fresh, new-firmware RAD can prove its own successor-path proof.

For the SITE-S window specifically: which OTHER rad-* provides the management-controller "proof" for SITE-S site's controllers? Rad-SITE-S — its OWN controller (INFRA-4 iDRAC SOL) — so BEFORE flashing INFRA-217, run a SOL attach to INFRA-4's iDRAC via INFRA-217. That's the pre-window task satisfying the gate ordering — the advisory is asking exactly this. Actually we already DID similar rad proofs previously per the mental model/persona? There's also an "external RAD public-path proof" involved: "Gateway package work and reboot recovery require a fresh public-path proof: workstation to the RAD's active external address...then controller/SOL through that trusted RAD session." — so the SOL GOAL at this point is "prove the site's OOB path still works through the just-flashed unit". So my plan's step 1 (pre-flash SOL) gets a more exact statement; then POST-right flash = THIS build's proof step.

This order update is a legitimate plan refinement — do it as one surgical edit to the plan's per-appliance sequence + ask no new approval (doc-only). Note deltas:

1. Break step 1 into (a) pre-window fresh public-path through the ACTIVE public rad-<site> + (b) a SOL-attach proof via that same RAD (before any transaction — the AGENTS blocking prerequisite stated in gateway-context; for RAD windows it transfers to: prove the pre-flash OOB layer on which post-flash recovery checks will be asserted).
2. Add explicit forward/lite recovery scope note: record that a hard-flash failure leaves THIS SITE'S OOB unit down until physical/on-site recovery (no in-band rescue from ANOTHER rad; sites are geo-independent), and that SITE-S's window runs first because the fleet's dependency map makes it the smallest blast radius? No actual dependency map — I chose SITE-S first on evidence-uncertainty reasons; keep.
3. Post-flash verification step already includes an OOB re-check but the exact language "controller/SOL path usable through the RAD" moves BEFORE the reboot (as the pre-window proof), and the post-reboot steps re-prove.

Edit the plan: renumber steps cleanly (I'll rewrite the "Per-appliance sequence" section 9-47 wholesale via one surgical set of PUT/CUT operations; to avoid the residue-hell, rebuild the whole list block in one PUT with final content. The block spans lines 9-47ish - a single PUT block op replacing lines 9.=47 might touch too much… per edit contract PUT N*:-style block resolution applies to "syntactic blocks"; markdown numbered list = less defined. Safest: read the CURRENT file once; then rewrite lines 9-48 in a single PUT with clean numbered sequence; verify with re-read; hash once.

Also update the somWindow order note "which rad-* hop provides proof for SITE-S": say the proof hops THROUGH INFRA-158 itself pre-flash (it's SITE-S's own OOB device — the only OOB unit per site), so pre-flash proof intentionally goes through the unit being flashed (captures gate state pre), while post-flash proof repeat through the same unit confirms restored function. State that literally in the plan. (There's no OTHER rad path to SITE-S; sites are independent.)

messages.content:
Opengear recovery usually works by **forcing the bootloader into network-recovery mode** with the **erase/reset button**, then serving the recovery image over **DHCP/BOOTP and TFTP** from a separate PC.[1][2][22]

The key idea is:
- **Hold the erase/reset button while powering on** the unit to trigger recovery mode.[1][2]
- Use a PC on the **same subnet** with a **DHCP server** and **TFTP server** prepared with the Opengear recovery image.[1][2]
- The bootloader loads a **minimal runtime image into RAM** over TFTP, then you can usually finish restoration through the device’s temporary web interface.[1][2]

What the Opengear recovery guide says:
- The bootloader supports loading a runtime image into RAM using **TFTP**.[1]
- For the net-boot/recovery flow, you should **turn the device off**, **depress the erase button**, and **turn it on while still holding the erase button**.[1]
- The guide indicates you then browse to the device’s recovery web interface to upload a working firmware image.[1]

A practical serial-console recovery workflow, based on Opengear guidance and field reports, is:
- Connect a **serial console** at **115200 baud** so you can watch boot messages and confirm recovery mode.[14][53]
- Hold the **erase/reset** button during power-on until the device enters recovery mode.[1][14]
- Run a local **DHCP + TFTP** server on your computer and place the correct Opengear **recovery image** in the TFTP directory.[1][2]
- After the recovery image boots, use the temporary web UI to upload the full firmware.[1][2]

If the firmware is merely corrupted, this method is commonly enough to **unbrick** the unit; however, if the bootloader itself is damaged, network recovery may not start and you would need a lower-level repair path, which is not covered by the Opengear recovery guide.[1][2]

If you want, I can turn this into a **step-by-step recovery checklist** for a specific Opengear model such as **CM41xx, ACM500x, OM1200/OM1300, or IM4200**.

{"content":"# RAD firmware rollout plan — one appliance at a time (2026-09-06)

Implements the 2026-09-06 decision (direct 4.x → 5.5.2, see
`rad_upgrade_decisions.2026-09-06.md`) inside issue `ORG-1/devops#13`. Each
appliance goes through these gates individually; no fleet-wide parallel work.

## Per-appliance sequence

1. **Pre-window OOB/SOL gate (BEFORE any transaction — AGENTS.md blocking
   prerequisite, restated for RAD windows):** fresh public-path proof
   workstation → the target RAD's ACTIVE public LTE address, then a short
   successful SOL/controller attach through that same RAD. For the SITE-S window
   this hop IS `INFRA-158` itself — it is the site's own OOB unit; no other
   RAD serves SITE-S (sites are independent), so the pre-flash SOL proof is
   captured pre-transaction and re-proven post-reboot on the new firmware.
2. **Recovery-scope record for the window:** the appliance being flashed IS
   the site's only OOB device; a hard-flash failure means no in-fleet rescue —
   recovery is the vendor's physical/bootloader path (step 6). Stated
   explicitly rather than over-promising in-band rescue.
3. **New pre-change captures** (one group per SSH session): `config.system`
   re-read for the FIPS-mode key state (5.x removes FIPS 140-2 support — a
   FIPS-enabled unit needs its target decided explicitly, not defaulted);
   `config -g config.openvpn` / tunnel-backend capture to identify what
   actually terminates `tun0` on SITE-D/SITE-Z/SITE-T (the incumbent backend lives
   within the pinned firmware's upgrade scope — confirm the config side before
   the window); on-box upgrade-verb CUSTH-31 (live evidence 2026-09-06: all five
   units probed directly — TOKEN-288 — `node-upgrade` and
   `fwupgrade` are absent on every train; only the unrelated
   `qmi-firmware-update` modem helper exists, so the on-board CLI is NOT the
   upgrade vehicle on this fleet; the non-destructive console-menu/`busybox`
   listing is re-checked once per unit at window time for any alternate local
   update verb — `ovpkg`/`firmware-update` — presence replaces the upload flow).
4. **Pre-change config backup** (downloaded from the unit immediately BEFORE
   its own transition; keep BOTH the 4.x backup for rollback and, after the
   upgrade, a fresh 5.5.2 backup — vendor rule: a config backup from another
   MAJOR version will not apply; the pre-change export is per-transition, not
   a reuse of the baseline card).
5. **Upgrade**: transfer the pinned image over the internal br0 management
   path, never pulled over metered cellular links; at transfer time confirm
   the SKU↔image mapping against the vendor release notes — TOKEN-153 =
   `acm7004-5-release-5.5.2.flash`, SITE-L = `acm700x-release-5.5.2.flash` — a
   mismatched image is the one failure mode that can leave a single-RAD site
   with no OOB path and no fleet fallback.
   Image staging: the pinned image is `scp`'d to the unit (prefer
   `/var/mnt/storage.nvlog` over `/tmp` tmpfs; `df -h` checked first), and its
   SHA1/MD5 compared against the vendor sidecar re-fetched at window
   open, then referenced by path.
   Transfer vehicle: the vendor-documented Web UI path —
   `readme-prior-to-upgrade-ACM.pdf` explicitly points at "Upgrading firmware
   using the web UI"; the REST v1.7 spec carries no firmware endpoints; the
   on-box CLI CUSTH-31 found no upgrade verb — so the upload runs as an SSH-run
   curl session ON THE APPLIANCE posting login + the multipart POST to its own
   127.0.0.1 web handler. Off-box IPv4 probes to :80/:443 were refused on SITE-S
   AND SITE-Z (fast RST, not misroute), hostname-based attempts refused likewise,
   and SITE-S exposes no global IPv6 space — the UI is appliance-local loopback
   only; an `ssh -L` port-forward to the unit's loopback is the confirmed
   equivalent if on-box curl proves awkward. The appliance credential is
   fetched from the Bitwarden vault at runtime and piped over SSH stdin —
   never argv, files, logs, or chat. First-use contract discovery (the upload
   form's action URL and the current per-session `csrf_token` — echoed from
   the authenticated session, not the anonymous-page `init` placeholder)
   runs in one credentialed probe session immediately before the first window
   and is recorded in the rollout log for later hops; the session is
   re-GET-verified via the cookie jar before the multipart upload is composed.
   SITE-L additionally: post-upgrade check that the -LMV SKU cellular stack still
   reaches carrier (vendor 5.x notes disable CDMA bands on -LMV SKUs;
   documented override `config.cellmodem.enable_cdma` if LTE behavior changes).
6. **Recovery route (documented BEFORE apply):** if the flash leaves the unit
   unbootable, the vendor recovery path is: power off → press and HOLD the
   erase/reset button → power on while holding it — the bootloader enters
   recovery mode, requests an address via BOOTP/DHCP, and TFTP-loads a minimal
   RAM runtime; from there the unit's temporary recovery web UI accepts the
   full firmware image (push the archived 4.x image for rollback, or re-push
   the same 5.5.2 image). Requirements: physical presence at that site's rack,
   a laptop/PC on the same subnet serving DHCP+TFTP, and the pinned/rollback
   image staged locally at the scene — recorded now so the first window
   carries its own recovery instead of assuming one exists remotely. If the
   bootloader itself is damaged (recovery mode never starts), the path is a
   vendor RMA/hardware repair — out of program scope. Console supervision
   runs at 115200 baud when a chase is required.
7. **Reboot**; verify post-boot:
   - `cat /etc/version` shows `5.5.2` with a vendor build stamp;
   - `config -g config.system` identity fields unchanged (hostname, timezone,
     model);
   - interface inventory: `br0` unchanged, `wwan0`/`wwan1` state live-queried,
     `tun0` present where it existed pre-upgrade;
   - SSH pinned-key login works (possible algorithm/key renegotiation noted by
     vendor 5.0.0's OpenSSH 7.7 → 9.5p1 jump — record the presented key
     fingerprints as a change event per AGENTS.md identity rules if these
     change);
   - **fresh post-reboot OOB/SOL gate**: the same public-path + SOL/controller
     attach proof re-run THROUGH THE NEW FIRMWARE (this restores the
     AGENTS.md blocking prerequisite for the next window on this site — the
     proof-through-RAD is now backed by 5.5.2, and the pre-flash capture in
     step 1 is the comparison point).
8. **RT discipline after the hop**: allocation updates reference the
   POST-upgrade interface names only (live re-read first; any drift becomes
   its own reconcile scope, never silently reusing pre-upgrade labels).
9. Resume package/monitoring automation if any runtime masks were used.

## Execution order

SITE-S → SITE-T → SITE-L → SITE-Z → SITE-D (smallest evidence-uncertainty first; SITE-D last
since its current firmware is already 4.13.6 and it carries the most recent
host-key rotation history).

## Post-upgrade homogeneous state

- All five on 5.5.2; per-unit choices (SNMP enablement, firewall shape, telnet
  state) UNCHANGED in this cycle per decision #2 — the deltas remain
  documented in `rad_config_baseline.2026-09-06.md` and are out of scope
  unless a separate later approval chain executes them.
- The OpenVPN-OOB enablement decision (per-RAD listener) is a SEPARATE
  approval scope after the firmware baseline exists fleet-wide.
- RackTables reconcile (attributes + carrier-prefix naming) executed on its
  own approved blocks; SITE-T object-type/naming harmonization remains
  proposal-only.

## Rollback

- Config restore within the same major version (pre-upgrade 4.x backup), or
  firmware re-flash of the archived 4.x image if needed (see step 6's
  recovery vehicle); fleet impact is limited to the individual unit because
  the OOB plane was never shared.
- Vendor rule carried verbatim: back up the configuration before the upgrade;
  if there are upgrade issues, revert to 4.x and re-apply the 4.x backup
  config.

#!/bin/sh
#
# Applies power to cellmodem according to /etc/config/SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf
#
# For one-shot control, run this script with the on/off parameter but
# keep in mind that the cellmodem's power state can be changed at the
# next system reboot based on the SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf file
#
# For permanent control, run the following command:
#    config -s config.cellmodem.hardware.disable={on,off} -r dialin
# and reboot the device
COMMAND=$1
read vendorproduct _ < /etc/version
case $vendorproduct in
    */ACM700* | */LES160* | */B093-* )
        product_setpower () { gpioset 0-0022 11=$1; } # USB_INT_5V_EN
	;;
    */IM72xx | */LES17* | TrippLite/B098-* )
        product_setpower () { gpioset f1010100.gpio 29=$1; } # USB_INT_5V_EN
	;;
    *)
	echo "$0: no cellmodem power control on $vendorproduct" >&2
	exit 1
	;;
esac
if [ "$COMMAND" = "off" ] || grep -sq ^CELLMODEM_DISABLE=yes /etc/config/SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf; then
    logger -t info "Powering down cellular modem"
    product_setpower 0
elif [ "$COMMAND" = "on" ] || ! grep -sq ^CELLMODEM_DISABLE=yes /etc/config/SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf; then
    logger -t info "Powering up cellular modem"
    product_setpower 1
fi

<advisory severity="nit" guidance="weigh, don't blindly obey">
Three tightenings: (1) The empty `==MM-HELP-POWER` section is likely grep vs help-output routing, not absence of the option — just run `mmcli -m 3 --set-power-state=on` directly and read the reply/error string itself; one bounded attempt beats parsing help on a trimmed build. (2) Before concluding 'cellctld is absent by design failure', grab a full unfiltered `ps -ax` — Opengear firmware often consolidates services under a few long-running binaries (the `portmanager Ss+` owning ttyUSB4 hints cellular I/O may be hosted inside an existing process rather than a separate `cellctld`); the process supervisor model matters for whether 'daemon missing' is even the right diagnosis. The repeated `Failed to detect running cellctld service` from conman suggests the detector and the daemon may have different naming — worth one look at how conman's check invokes it. (3) Good instinct writing the rail-cycle lever into the plan; record it as 'observed once on SITE-S' rather than fleet law, and have each remaining RAD window re-confirm the sequence — two warm reboots missing enumeration vs one rail-cycle revival is n=1 evidence, cheap to re-verify per unit at window start anyway.
</advisory>
<advisory severity="nit" guidance="weigh, don't blindly obey">
Good pivot to the decisive CUSTH-31. Two mechanics that matter for the result to be trustworthy: (1) `AT+COPS=?` CUSTH-9 commonly exceed ModemManager's internal serial-response timeout even when the CUSTH-31 itself completes — the `Serial command timed out` on the first read doesn't yet mean 'no operators'. After firing the CUSTH-31, wait ~60-90 s and re-read `AT+COPS?` and `AT!GSTATUS?` on index 4; a completed CUSTH-31 leaves visible residue (selected-operator line or a changed GMM state) even though the issuing call timed out. Judge on the second read, not the timeout. (2) Make sure the backgrounded job's outer `timeout` actually covers the full CUSTH-31 window — the first invocation wrapped mmcli in `timeout 25`, which truncates a CUSTH-31 designed for ~90 s; the bg job should use a matching-or-longer bound so you don't mistake a wrapper cutoff for an empty CUSTH-31. Interpretation once results land: operators listed but no camp → firmware/NVM reprofile is the justified rung; truly nothing after a full-window CUSTH-31 → antenna/coverage physical check at the rack leads, and the 4.12.3 rollback becomes the pragmatic fallback rather than more software churn.

<advisory severity="nit" guidance="weigh, don't blindly obey">
Reasonable convergence; three refinements before the hand-off lands: (1) One more cheap retry is actually justified by your own evidence — MM's `failed/sim-missing` is a *manager-side* verdict that frequently goes stale after a module reset while the card itself is fine (your CPIN READY read). Do this once inside the chosen route's pre-checks rather than as a separate round. (2) For the on-device route, Sierra/SWI9X50 modules on `qmi-firmware-update` commonly need the old/new pairing flags (`--update-old` + `--update-new`) or a two-step for full-package images — single `--update` with just the `.cwe` works for generic-only pushes but verify against `qmi-firmware-update --help` on the box before composing, exactly as you planned. #!/bin/sh
# This script has two modes
# ACTION=boot is called from /etc/rc at boot (before udev is started)
# ACTION=add is delay-triggered from udev-cellmodem when a potential cellmodem is detected
#            and should only be called when DEVTYPE=usb_device.
#            Note: This script will only be called once via udev. See scripts/udev-cellmodem
set -xv +e
if [ "$ACTION" = boot ]; then
	# Setup modem directory
	rm -rf /var/run/.modem/cellmodem*
	modprobe usbserial
	# Remove the services we used to keep in the main inittab
	# which was where rc.cellmodem used to put them.
	# Now edinittab puts them in /var/run/inittab
	# TODO: move this to migrate
	edinittab -n -f /etc/config/inittab del 'cellctld'
	edinittab    -f /etc/config/inittab del 'ledmon'
	exit 0
fi
# Check to see if cellmodem power is disabled, if that is the case we exit immediatley
#
# 1. rc starts udevd
# 2. rc calls rc.product > cellmodem-power script to power off cellmodem
# 3. udevd runs udev-cellmodem > rc.cellmodem
#
# There is no guarantee that #3 happens absolutely _after_ #2, so we also need to check
# if cellmodem has been disabled
# On the other hand, when #2 happens first, #3 won't take place at all
if [ -e /etc/config/SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf ]; then
	. /etc/config/SUBDOMAIN-2.examplenf
	if [ "$CELLMODEM_DISABLE" ]; then
		exit 0;
	fi
fi
# ignore non-USB invocations
if [ "$DEVTYPE" != usb_device ]; then
	exit 0
fi
# get MODEL as lowercase device string
MODEL=$(tr A-Z a-z </etc/version | sed -e 's, .*,,;s,.*/,,')
read Vendor       </sys$DEVPATH/idVendor
read ProdID       </sys$DEVPATH/idProduct
read Manufacturer </sys$DEVPATH/manufacturer
read Product      </sys$DEVPATH/product
# for debug
: Vendor="$Vendor" ProdID="$ProdID"
: Manufacturer="$Manufacturer" Product="$Product"

- The firmware image + PRI/carrier bundle = **one active pairing per module at a time** (the module's own `--modem-storage-index` slots are selectable, but that's a per-*window* state, not an automatic run-time behavior). There is **no vendor-supported auto-selection keyed to whichever SIM is currently in the slot**. Sierra's flash state machine changes image only on an explicit re-push or a preference change, followed by its own re-enumeration/reboot — it's not a hot per-SIM swap.

function.name: read
function.description:
Read files, directories, archives, SQLite, images, documents, internal resources, and web URLs via `path`.

<instruction>
- SHOULD parallelize independent reads.
- SHOULD use `read` (not browser) for web content; browser only when `read` can't deliver.
</instruction>

## Selectors — append `:<sel>` to `path` (e.g. `src/foo.ts:50-200`, `src/foo.ts:raw`, `db.sqlite:users:42`)

- `:50` / `:50-` — from line 50 | `:50-200` — inclusive | `:50+150` — 150 lines from 50 | `:-60` — last 60 lines | `:5-16,960-973` — multiple ranges
- `:raw` — verbatim, no anchors/prefixes | `:2-4:raw` / `:raw:2-4` — range + verbatim
- `:conflicts` — one line per unresolved git merge conflict block
- `:img` — rasterize a local `.svg`/`.svgz` as a PNG image; use when visual layout matters
- `?q=<question>` — image only (also `.svg:img?q=`, `attachment://N?q=`, `local://…?q=`): vision-model answer as text instead of pixels
- Videos (`.mp4`, `.mov`, `.mkv`, `.webm`, `.m4v`, `.avi`, `.wmv`) need system `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe`: bare read returns a preview grid plus metadata (resolution, codecs, duration, fps); `:412` extracts frame 412, `:1h5m42s`/`:90s`/`:01:23` seeks to a timestamp

## Source kinds

- Parseable code, no selector → structural summary (declarations only, body elided). Footer names recovery selector — re-issue ONLY those ranges.
- File + selector → `[foo.ts#1A2B]` snapshot header + numbered lines. Copy `[FILENAME#TAG]` for anchored edits; NEVER fabricate the tag.
- Directory → depth-limited dirent listing.
- SQLite (`.sqlite`, `.sqlite3`, `.db`, `.db3`): `file.db` (tables), `file.db:table` (schema+rows), `file.db:table:key` (by PK), `?limit=`/`?where=`/`?q=SELECT`.
- Archives (`.zip` family incl. `.jar`/`.apk`/`.whl`, `.tar` incl. `.tar.{gz,bz2,xz,zst}`, `.rar`, `.7z`, `.iso`, `.cab`, `.deb`/`.rpm`/`.cpio`/`.ar`/`.a`, `.lzh`/`.arj`, `.asar`; single-stream `.gz`/`.bz2`/`.xz`/`.zst`): `archive.ext:path/inside/archive` reads a member.
- Documents → extracted text. Notebooks → editable cells. Images → decoded inline; `img.png?q=<question>` asks a vision model and returns text (spares context; works on any model). Videos → preview grid plus metadata. SVGs read as text unless `:img` is specified. `:raw` bypasses converters.
- URLs → reader-mode clean text/markdown; `:raw` → untouched HTML. Bare `host:port` needs trailing slash.
- Internal URIs — all schemes take selectors. `artifact://<id>` recovers spilled output; page with `:N-M`/`:raw:N-M`.
- `ssh://host/<path>` reads remote file/dir (UTF-8, ≤1 MiB); bare `ssh://` lists hosts; writable with `write` and searchable with `grep`.
  Literal `:`, `?`, `#` → percent-encode (`%3A`/`%3F`/`%23`). Requires a verified POSIX shell on the remote host. For Windows or other unsupported hosts, use `bash` with a remote SSH command or mount with `sshfs`.

<critical>
Summary footer names elided ranges? Re-issue ONLY those ranges. NEVER guess `..`/`…` content.
</critical>

path.description: Local path, internal URI (e.g. memory://, skill://), or URL. Inline selectors are supported.

function.name: bash
function.description:
Runs commands in a persistent shell.

Use ONLY for one binary or a short pipeline that computes a fact (`wc -l`, `sort | uniq -c`, `diff`).
Inline scripts, heredocs, `$(…)`, complex control flow/quoting, and non-trivial pipelines → `eval`.

<instruction>
- Set `cwd` instead of `cd`; use `env: { NAME: "…" }` for multiline/quote-heavy values.
- `pty: true` only for terminal interaction (`sudo`, `ssh`).
- Order-dependent commands use `&&` in one call; independent calls may run concurrently.
- Internal URIs (`skill://`, `agent://`, …) auto-resolve to paths.
- aux utils available: mkdir, wc, sort, comm, diff, uniq, base64, cmp, md5sum, sha{1,224,256,384,512}sum, b2sum, basename, dirname, readlink, realpath, touch, stat, date, mktemp, seq, yes, printenv, truncate, tac, nproc, uname, whoami, hostname, which, ps, pgrep, pkill, pidwait, top, cut, tee, tr, paste, sed, xargs, jq, rm, mv, ln, ts, sponge, ifne, isutf8, combine, errno
- `async: true` defers a finite command's result; it does not extend `timeout`.
</instruction>

<critical>
- NEVER use shell `grep`/`rg`; use built-in `grep`.
- List directories with `read` and find paths with `glob`; NEVER use `ls`/`find`.
- Avoid `head`, `tail`, and redirection: output is captured, truncated, and linked as `artifact://<id>`.
- Services, watchers, debuggers, and REPLs MUST use `hub` (`op:"start"`).
</critical>

Long foreground calls may auto-background by the configured threshold and deliver later.
`timeout: 0` disables the job deadline; otherwise `timeout` sets it without extending foreground waiting.
No truncation footer means the displayed output is complete.

function.name: edit
function.description:
Line-anchored patch language: name original lines/gaps to replace, insert, cut, or paste; then give new content. `:` headers take `+` body rows; colonless paste `PUT`, `CUT`, `REM`, `MV` take none.

<headers>
Section: `[PATH#TAG]`; `TAG`: 4-hex snapshot from latest `read`/`search`, REQUIRED each section. New files: `write`; hashline edits existing files only.
</headers>

<ops>
`PUT N.=M:`: replace original inclusive lines N–M with body.
`PUT N*:`: replace syntactic block beginning N; closing line resolved.
`PUT <N:` insert body rows before line N (`PUT <1:` = file head).
`PUT >N:` insert body rows after line N (`PUT >$:` = file tail).
`PUT >N*:`: insert after block N's end, at sibling depth. Append inside block: `PUT >M:`.
`PUT <N @name` / `PUT >N @name` paste register `@name` at the gap before/after line N; omit `@name` for the anonymous register.
`PUT N.=M @name` / `PUT N* @name` paste `@name` over the range / resolved block; `@name` required here.
`CUT N.=M` / `CUT N*`: delete and capture inclusive lines N–M / block N; anonymous or given `@name`.
`REM`: delete section file. `MV DEST`: move/rename (quote paths with spaces); prior edits apply to source, final content to `DEST`.
Single line: `PUT N.=N:` / `CUT N.=N`. Ranges name original inclusive touched lines; body length irrelevant.
</ops>

<body-rows>
Only below `:` headers. Row: verbatim `+TEXT` (leading whitespace preserved); `+`: blank. NEVER `-old`, bare, or context rows: range deletes; body is final content. Keep line: exclude it from every range. Literal initial `-`/`+`: `- item` → `+- item`; `+ item` → `++ item`.
</body-rows>

<rules>
- Numbers and `#TAG`: latest `read`/`search` `LINE:TEXT`; numbers are original, never shifted by hunks.
- Each edit renumbers and changes `#TAG` → next numbers from edit response or fresh `read`.
- Touch displayed lines only; undisplayed hunks REJECTED. Far from read window: re-`read`; confirm construct.
- Elisions UNSEEN: `…`, `..`, collapsed `N-M:` rows. NEVER hunk in/across one; `read` first.
- NEVER start/end range mid-expression or mid-block.
- Ranges: changed lines only; NEVER widen over keepers. Non-adjacent changes: separate hunks.
- Whole construct: `PUT N*:`; internal lines: `PUT N.=M:`.
- `PUT N*:` resolves exactly node N. Leading TOKEN-703 are separate nodes: point N at first decorator to include both. Standalone line-comments never swept: use `PUT N.=M:`.
- Block ops: opening line of multi-line construct, NEVER closer, last line, bare inner statement. One statement: plain `PUT N.=N:` / `CUT N.=N` / `PUT >N:`. At closer: `PUT >M:`.
- Markdown headings are block openers. Block op on `##`/`###`: whole section through deeper headings to next same/higher heading. After section `PUT >N*:`: end body with blank line to separate next heading.
- Pure addition: `PUT <N:` / `PUT >N:`, NEVER widened `PUT N.=M:`.
- Move: `CUT`+`PUT`; `CUT 5.=9 @fn` → `@fn`, `PUT >40 @fn` pastes. Single call-local move: unlabeled `CUT` + `PUT >40`. Named registers persist across edit calls.
- NEVER format/restyle with this tool; run project formatter.
</rules>

<example>
`read` output shape:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
1:def greet(name):
2:    msg = "Hello, " + name
3:    print(msg)
4:greet("world")
```

Edit, then move:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
PUT 1.=3:
+def greet(name):
+    print(f"Hi, {name}")
MV lib/greet.py
```

Markdown bullets — file receives `- task`:
```
[PLAN.md#A1B2]
PUT >2:
+- task
+  - nested task
```

Move `greet` to sibling file via named register; flows across sections:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
CUT 1* @fn
[other.py#3C4D]
PUT <1 @fn
```

`PUT 1*:` resolves lines 1–3 (`def` through `print(msg)`); line 4 separate, remains:
```
[greet.py#A1B2]
PUT 1*:
+def greet(name):
+    print(f"Hello, {name}")
```

Decorator/doc-comment separate block: point N at decorator to include both; anchoring `def` line 2 orphans `@cache`:
```
[svc.py#C3D4]
PUT 1*:
+@cache
+def load(key):
+    return store[key]
```
</example>

<anti-patterns>
# WRONG — empty `PUT` to delete. RIGHT: `CUT 4.=4`
PUT 4.=4:

# WRONG — range sized to the post-edit content. RIGHT: `PUT 1.=1:` (body length irrelevant)
PUT 1.=2:
+def greet(name):

# WRONG — `-` rows / bare context lines do not exist; the range deletes, the body is only new content.
PUT 3.=3:
    msg = "Hello, " + name
-   print(msg)
+   return msg
# RIGHT
PUT 3.=3:
+   return msg

# WRONG — pure insertion as a widened `PUT`: retyped keepers get dropped (here line 4).
PUT 2.=4:
+    msg = "Hello, " + name
+    extra = compute(name)
+    print(msg)
# RIGHT — touch nothing you keep.
PUT >2:
+    extra = compute(name)

# WRONG — `PUT >N*:` anchored on the closing delimiter / last visible line. RIGHT: plain `PUT >M:`
PUT >3*:
+after()
# RIGHT
PUT >3:
+after()

# WRONG — body rows under register PUT; register pastes take no body. RIGHT: bodyless `PUT >20 @fn`.
PUT >20 @fn:
+function f() {}
</anti-patterns>

<critical>
1. RE-GROUND AFTER EVERY EDIT: edits renumber and change `#TAG`; take next numbers from edit response or fresh `read`. Stale tag/surprise: STOP; re-`read`.
2. RANGES TIGHT: changed lines only. Whole construct: `PUT N*:`.
3. BODY FINAL CONTENT: every row starts `+`; Markdown bullet: `+- item`, not `- item`.
</critical>

function.name: eval
function.description:
Run one step of code in a persistent kernel. State persists across calls and `task` subagents.
Eval `agent()` children use independent kernels.

Work incrementally: imports → define → test → use, each its own cell. Re-run setup ONLY after `reset`, kernel crash.
Two or more independent items → named `workpool()` + `.push(…)`; poll outside eval with `hub wait` on the pool name. Handles + `wait()` are for dependency-coupled results.

Top-level `await` works; `asyncio.run(…)` raises error.
JS runs under **Bun**: globals (`SUBDOMAIN-2.examplele`, `Bun.write`, `Bun.$`, `fetch`, `Buffer`) available; top-level `await`/`return` work.

On error, fix and re-run only the failing step.

<prelude>
Python: sync, kwargs. JS: async, ONE trailing object literal, never positional.
```
display(value) → None        print(value, ...) → None
read(path, offset?=1, limit?=None) → str
write(path, content) → str
env(key?=None, value?=None) → str | None | dict
output(*ids, format?="raw", query?=None, offset?=None, limit?=None) → str | dict | list[dict]
await tool.<name>(args) → unknown
    Invoke any session tool; `args` = its parameter object. Async: `await tool.read({...})`.
completion(prompt, model?="default"|"smol"|"slow", system?=None, schema?=None) → CompletionHandle
    Oneshot, stateless (no history/tools); returns immediately. `.wait()` → str (parsed object with `schema`). `model`: "smol" fast | "default" session | "slow" most capable.
agent(prompt, agent?="task", label?=None, schema?=None, schemaMode?="permissive", isolated?=None, apply?=None, merge?=None, tools?=None) → AgentHandle
    Spawns a background subagent and returns immediately. `agent` selects a discovered agent; omit it to use `task`. Handle: `.id`, `.handle` ("agent://<id>"), `.status`, `.done()`, `.wait(timeout?)` → final text (parsed with `schema`), `.send(message)`, `.cancel()`, `.output()`. Unwaited results auto-deliver like async jobs. `schema` overrides agent/session schemas; `isolated` requests a worktree; `apply`/`merge` control its changes. `tools`: names of your @tool-defined tools the child may call.
    JS: ONE trailing object — agent(prompt, { agent, label, schema, schemaMode, isolated, apply, merge, tools }).
wait(handles, timeout?=None, raise_errors?=True) → list
    Barrier over agent/completion handles, results in input order. `raise_errors=False` keeps the error in its slot. JS: wait(handles, { timeout, raiseErrors }).
workpool(agent?=None, name?=None, context?=None, tools?=None) → WorkPool
    Default for 2+ independent items. `.push(*items)`; `.status()`; `.peek()`; `.close()`. Pool name = async job id; results auto-deliver, or poll outside eval with `hub wait` and `ids:[pool.name]`. `SUBDOMAIN-3.exampleeshAgents=true` uses a new agent per item.
@tool / tool(fn, name=None, description=None)tool(fn, { name?, description?, parameters? })
    Define a tool that runs in this kernel (schema inferred from type hints); reference by name in `task` items' `tools`, `agent(tools=…)`, `workpool(tools=…)`. `SUBDOMAIN-2.examplefined()`, `tool.undefine(name)`.
log(message) → None         phase(title) → None
budget → `budget.total` (ceiling or None), `budget.spent()`, `budget.remaining()``await budget.total()`, `await budget.spent()`, `await budget.remaining()`; ceiling `+Nk` advisory, `+Nk!` hard.
```
</prelude>

Drive real Chromium tabs from JavaScript or Python Eval with the global `browser` object.

<instruction>
- Static content? Use `read`. Use `browser` for JavaScript execution, authenticated sessions, and interactive actions.
- JavaScript: `await browser.open(options)` returns a `BrowserTab`; `browser.tab(name)` returns an existing handle; `await browser.close(options)` releases tabs.
- Python: `await browser.open(name=…, url=…)`, synchronous `browser.tab(name)`, and `await browser.close(name=…)`. Python methods accept keyword arguments.
- `open` options: `name`, `url`, `app`, `viewport`, `wait_until`, `dialogs`, `timeout`.
- `close` options: `name`, `all`, `kill`, `timeout`.
- Direct tab helpers:
  - Navigation: `url`, `title`, `goto`.
  - Inspection: `observe`, `ariaSnapshot`, `screenshot`, `extract`.
  - Interaction: `click`, `type`, `fill`, `press`, `scroll`, `drag`, `scrollIntoView`, `select`, `uploadFile`.
  - Waiting: `waitFor`, `waitForSelector`, `waitForUrl`.
  - Page execution: `evaluate`.
- `SUBDOMAIN-2.example(n)` / `tab.ref("e5")` return `BrowserElement` handles supporting `click`, `type`, `fill`, `press`, `hover`, `focus`, `select`, `uploadFile`, `scrollIntoView`, `boundingBox`, `isVisible`, `isHidden`, and `evaluate`. A string passed to `BrowserElement.evaluate` is a function expression invoked with the element as its first argument.
- JavaScript `await tab.run(fnOrCode, { args?, timeout? })` runs a function or code string. Functions receive `{ tab, page, browser, wait, assert }`; cell closures are not captured. Plain data, functions, and `RegExp` values are supported in `args`.
- Python `await tab.run(code, timeout=…)` accepts a JavaScript code string only. Direct Python helpers use the same method names; keyword arguments become a trailing JavaScript options object.
- `tab.run` executes in an isolated JavaScript tab runtime with raw Puppeteer `page`/`browser`, ordinary Eval helpers, and full Bun/Node + tool-bridge access. It is not sandboxed.
- Direct helpers and `tab.run` return real structured values. Nonempty inner `display` text prints in the outer Eval cell; screenshots surface as Eval images.
- Selectors accept CSS plus Puppeteer `aria/…`, `text/…`, `xpath/…`, and `pierce/…` query handlers.
- Navigation and re-renders invalidate observed ids and refs. Re-observe, then act in the same cell.
- Use `SUBDOMAIN-2.examplelect` for `<select>` elements; `SUBDOMAIN-2.examplell` does not support them.
- Raw request interception lasts only for the current `tab.run`.

Application modes:
- `app.path`: spawn the specified browser or Electron executable.
- `app.cdp_url`: attach to an existing CDP endpoint.
- `app.relay: true`: drive the user's Chrome through the omp relay. `app.target` selects a tab by URL/title substring; without it, the visible tab is adopted. Opening with `url` navigates that adopted tab.
- Relay sessions are the user's real logged-in browser. Sites attribute actions to the user. Name a target or create a dedicated tab; NEVER navigate the visible tab without authorization.
- Closing releases the managed tab. It never closes relay/CDP-attached pages. Spawned browsers remain open unless `kill: true`.
</instruction>

<examples>
```javascript
const tab = await browser.open({ name: "docs", url: "https://SUBDOMAIN-2.example" });
const observed = await tab.observe();
await SUBDOMAIN-2.example(observed.elements[0].id).click();
const title = await tab.run(async ({ tab }, suffix) => (await tab.title()) + suffix, { args: ["!"] });
await tab.close();
```

```python
tab = await browser.open(name="docs", url="https://SUBDOMAIN-2.example")
observed = await tab.observe()
await SUBDOMAIN-2.example(observed["elements"][0]["id"]).click()
title = await tab.run("return await tab.title();", timeout=30)
await tab.close()
```
</examples>

<critical>
- MUST open a tab before direct use; `browser.tab(name)` does not open one.
- Default to `tab.observe()`; use screenshots for visual confirmation.
- `tab.run` has full Bun/Node and tool-bridge access; it is not sandboxed.
- Relay and CDP actions operate on real user sessions.
</critical>
<dag>
Acyclic waves of handles:
- **Name nodes.** `h = agent(…)` returns at once; `h.handle` is `agent://<id>`.
- **Wire edges.** Put an upstream `.wait()` result or `.handle` in the downstream prompt. Bulk: `write("local://<name>.md", …)`.
- **`wait(hs)`** = wave barrier. Open-ended item streams → `workpool()`.
- **Isolate failure.** `wait(hs, raise_errors=False)` keeps a failure in its slot; only that subtree degrades.
- **Acyclic only.** No node waits on its own descendant.
</dag>

<critical>
Prior top-level names survive into the next cell — reuse; NEVER re-import/re-declare. Re-read only if file changed since last read.
</critical>

<examples>
# First call — set up once
<example>
eval(language="py", title="imports", code="""import json
from pathlib import Path""")
</example>
# Second call — reuse, do NOT re-import
<example>
eval(language="py", title="load config", code="""data = json.loads(read('package.json'))
display(data)""")
</example>
# Third call — reuse the loaded config
<example>
eval(language="py", title="CUSTH-3 deps", code="display(sorted(data['dependencies']))")
</example>
</examples>

language.description: runtime: "py" for the IPython kernel, "js" for the persistent JS VM

code.description: code to run in this eval call, verbatim. Use top-level await freely.

title.description: short label shown in transcript (e.g. "imports", "load config")

timeout.description: timeout for this eval call in seconds; 0 disables the cell timeout

reset.description: wipe this language's kernel before running. Other languages are untouched.

function.name: glob
function.description:
Globs files, directories, and path-backed internal URLs with fast pattern matching.

<instruction>
- `path`: glob, file, directory, or path-backed internal URL; separate targets with `;` (`src/**/*.ts; test/**/*.ts`).
- `memory://` glob patterns are supported. `ssh://` has no local path; use `read`. Other internal URLs accept exact paths only.
- `gitignore` defaults `true`. Set `false` for ignored files such as `.env*`, logs, or build output.
- `hidden` defaults `true`; pair it with `gitignore: false` for ignored dotfiles.
</instruction>

<output>
Matches are newest-first and grouped by directory; directories end in `/`.
</output>

<avoid>
Open-ended multi-round discovery → Task + scout.
</avoid>

<examples>
# Glob files
<example i="…">
src/**/*.ts
</example>
# Multiple targets — semicolon-delimited list
<example i="…">
src/**/*.ts; test/**/*.ts
</example>
# Glob gitignored files like .env
<example>
glob(i="…", path=".env*", gitignore=False)
</example>
# Glob directories matching a name (returns both files and dirs; directories are suffixed with `/`)
<example i="…">
**/tests
</example>
</examples>

path.description: glob, file, or directory to search — a single path or a semicolon-delimited list ("src/**/*.ts; test/**/*.ts"). Omitted -> searches the workspace root (".")

function.name: grep
function.description:
Searches files/internal URLs: Rust regex, PCRE2 fallback.

<instruction>
- `path`: known files, directories, globs, internal URLs; roots `;`-separated.
- Broad searches may time out → narrow scope or use `glob` first.
- One-file line selector: `src/foo.ts:50-100`; never selects search root.
- Literal `\n` or `\\n` enables cross-line patterns.
</instruction>

<critical>
- MUST use instead of shell `grep`/`rg`.
- Open-ended multi-round search MUST use Task + scout, not chained calls.
</critical>

path.description: file, directory, glob, internal URL, or "<file>:<lines>" selector to search; pass several as a semicolon-delimited list ("src; tests"). Omitted -> searches the workspace root (".")

skip.description: files to skip before collecting results — use to paginate when the prior call hit the file limit

function.name: task
function.description:
Delegate work to background subagents by passing multiple items in a single `tasks[]` batch.
Execution does not block — you receive IDs immediately.

# Async Job Contract
- Results auto-deliver. A settled `hub jobs`/`hub wait` snapshot is the delivery; no duplicate `async-result` follows.
- Job IDs are process-local and expire roughly five minutes after settlement. Afterward, use the agent ID with `hub send`, `agent://<id>`, or `history://<id>`.
- With `outputSchema`, a result's parsed payload — when present — is served at `agent://<id>` (fields via `agent://<id>?q=.<field>`) regardless of validity; a schema-violating (invalid) result also previews the payload inline in the auto-delivered follow-up.
- `completed` means successful yield/job exit, not artifact acceptance. Verify claimed changes.

# Task Design
- **Agent typing:** Pick each item's most specific available agent. Read-only research MUST run on `scout` (faster model). Omit `agent` when the spawn-policy default is the best fit; otherwise pass the specialist explicitly.
- **No overhead:** Each `task` MUST instruct its agent to skip formatters, linters, and project-wide test suites. Run those once at the end.
- **One-pass:** Prefer agents that investigate AND edit in one pass; spin a read-only scout only when affected files are genuinely unknown.
- **Overlap:** Parallelize independent ownership. Same-file edits are not guaranteed to merge. Have siblings coordinate through `hub` before editing shared files. Name one integration owner and serialize only the irreducibly shared mutation boundary. Every concurrent batch has two prerequisites:
  1. Every task MUST skip validation (build/lint/tests) — validating mid-flight blocks agents on each other's edits.
  2. Decide cross-task contracts up front (e.g. the interface A implements and B consumes) and state them in the batch `context`, not left for agents to negotiate.

# Inputs
- `context`: Shared project state, constraints, and contracts. Applies to the entire batch; do not duplicate this background into individual tasks.
- `tasks[]`: Array of subagents to spawn.
  - `name`: A stable CamelCase identifier (≤32 chars), used to address the agent (IRC, job ids). Generated automatically if omitted.
  - `agent`: The agent type to spawn (e.g. `scout`, `reviewer`).
    Omitting `agent` selects the spawn-policy default (`task`). Use it only when that agent fits the task.
    NEVER pass the spawn-policy default explicitly. Only omit it after checking the available agents below.
  - `task`: Complete, self-contained instructions. One-liners or missing acceptance criteria are PROHIBITED.
  - `tools`: Names of eval-defined tools (`@tool` in Python, `tool(fn, {…})` in JS) to expose to this subagent; each runs inside your kernel when the subagent calls it.
  - `outputSchema`: Invocation-specific JSON Schema. Overrides the selected agent and parent-session schemas.
  - `schemaMode`: `"permissive"` (default) accepts a retry-exhausted invalid result with a warning; `"strict"` fails it.

# Communication
Subagents start blank — no conversation history. Parent-to-subagent IRC delivered immediately as steering.
Pass large payloads via `local://<path>` URIs, NEVER inline text.

# Format Contracts
`context` format:
# Goal         ← what the batch accomplishes
# Constraints  ← rules and session decisions
# Contract     ← shared interfaces

`task` format:
# Target       ← exact files and symbols; explicit non-goals
# Change       ← step-by-step add/remove/rename; APIs and patterns
# Acceptance   ← observable result; no project-wide commands

# Available Agents
Pick the most specific agent. Omit `agent` only when the spawn-policy default is that agent.
### scout (READ-ONLY)
MUST be used for exploratory codebase research, rapid code analysis, and broad pattern searches. Fast read-only scout returning compressed context for handoff.
Use ONLY for investigation; do edits yourself or assign to a writing agent.

### reviewer
Code review specialist for quality/security analysis
### security-reviewer
Read-only security specialist for evidence-backed repository vulnerability discovery
### task
General-purpose subagent with full capabilities for delegated multi-step tasks
### sonic
Low-reasoning agent for strictly mechanical updates or data collection only

function.name: hub
function.description:
Agent coordination: peer messaging, background-job control, and supervised long-running processes. Main agent is `Main`; subagents inherit task ID.
Use `op: "list"` to discover live peers. Default is running+idle plus TOKEN-704 counts — never an unbounded parked name dump. Pass `status: "parked"` for parked archaeology; optional `limit` bounds rows (default 32, max 100). Address peers by exact roster ID — NEVER invent names. `send` to a known parked id still revives it; `history://<id>` and `agent://<id>` stay readable.

# Messaging & Jobs

Background jobs auto-deliver when they finish. You NEVER need to poll; if `jobs`/`wait` observes a settled job first, that snapshot is the delivery and suppresses duplicate `async-result`.

- **The user is NOT a peer.** `Main` answers the user ONLY in a plain text block; a `send` shows them a tool-card preview (2 lines while collapsed). Thinking is not output either.
- **`send`** (with `to`): fire-and-forget, NEVER blocks. Delivery receipts (`delivered`/`failed`) immediate; `failed` → peer gone, don't retry.
  Sending wakes `idle`/`parked` peers. Answering: lead with answer, NEVER quote, set `replyTo`.
- **Format**: plain prose ONLY. No JSON status objects. Share paths via `local://`/`artifact://` URLs, not pasted blobs.
- **`wait`**: use ONLY when completely blocked with no other work. Returns on the FIRST of: an incoming message, a watched job finishing, the wait window elapsing, or a steering interrupt — NOT when all jobs finish; re-issue to keep waiting.
  - Bare `wait` watches every running job AND incoming messages. NEVER pass an array of every running ID; `ids` narrows to specific jobs, `from` to one peer (or use `await: true` on send).
  - A **user** message arriving as steering is not a wake reason to poll past: answer it in a text block BEFORE re-issuing `wait`. Parent/peer steering is answered with `send`; advisor and budget steers need no reply.
- **`inbox`**: drain queued messages without blocking.
- **`cancel`**: kill background jobs by `ids` when they have hung, stalled, or are no longer needed. Returns immediately.
- **`jobs`**: status snapshot of every job without waiting. A settled row consumes auto-delivery. Also names running subagents with no job entry — coordinate with those via `send`.
- Job rows are process-local and expire roughly five minutes after settlement. Afterward, use the agent ID with `send`, `agent://<id>`, or `history://<id>`.
- `completed` means successful yield/job exit, not artifact acceptance. Verify claimed changes.
- NEVER use shell tools, grep, or read other sessions' files to figure out what a peer is doing. Message them directly.
- NEVER use hub messaging for something a tool can answer (e.g., grepping codebase, running a build).

# Processes

Project-scoped long-running processes shared by every omp instance in the same directory. A long-running service, watcher, debugger, REPL, or process needing later input MUST use `op:"start"`, not `bash`.

- **`start`** launches `application` + `args` directly. `cwd` defaults to the session directory; `pty` defaults true.
  - `ready.log` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag; PCRE inline modifiers such as `(?i)` are REJECTED — use `[Rr]eady` instead. `ready.port` is a TCP port. Both supplied? BOTH MUST pass. `ready.timeout` is seconds. Readiness MUST be observed; process creation alone is not readiness.
  - Names are unique per project directory. A completed name MAY be started again; a live name MUST be stopped or restarted.
  - `restart` policy defaults `no`; `on-failure` and `always` use bounded backoff.
  - `persist: true` opts out of last-omp teardown; `detached: true` survives broker shutdown and all omp exits (implies persist, disables PTY input). Omit both unless their survival guarantees are required.
- **`ps`**, **`logs`**, **`wait`** (with `name`), **`send`** (with `name`), **`stop`**, **`restart`**, and **`describe`** address the stable `name`.
- **`logs`** defaults to the last 100 lines. `head: true` reads the beginning. `grep` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag (no inline modifiers such as `(?i)`). `follow: true` waits for output after `cursor`; reuse the returned cursor on the next call.
- **`wait`** with `name` blocks until readiness/exit/`pattern` or `timeout` (seconds). `pattern` is a JavaScript `RegExp` compiled with the `u` flag (no inline modifiers such as `(?i)`).
- **`send`** with `name`: `text` writes stdin (`enter` defaults true); `keys` supports ENTER, TAB, ESCAPE, CTRL_C, CTRL_D, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT; `signal` supports SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP, SIGQUIT, SIGKILL. PTY input is serialized; writes share one input stream.
- **`stop`** performs graceful process-tree termination before hard-kill; NEVER kill an unverified PID through bash. **`restart`** reuses the retained launch spec.

<examples>
# List peers
<example i="…">
list
</example>
# Inspect parked peer history
<example>
hub(i="…", op="list", status="parked")
</example>
# Fire-and-forget DM — same send wakes idle/parked peers
<example>
hub(i="…", op="send", to="AuthLoader", message="Still touching src/server/auth.ts? I need to add a 401 path.")
</example>
# Round-trip when you cannot proceed without the answer
<example>
hub(i="…", op="send", to="Main", message="JWT or session cookies for the auth flow?", await=True)
</example>
# Completely blocked: wait for the first finished job or incoming message
<example i="…">
wait
</example>
# Block until a specific peer answers
<example>
hub(i="…", op="wait", from="AuthLoader", timeoutMs=60000)
</example>
# Kill a hung background job
<example>
hub(i="…", op="cancel", ids=["bash_a1b2c3"])
</example>
# Snapshot every background job without waiting
<example i="…">
jobs
</example>
# Start a dev server and wait for its log banner and port
<example>
hub(i="…", op="start", name="web", application="bun", args=["run", "dev"], ready={"log": "Local:.*http", "port": 5173, "timeout": 30})
</example>
# Follow process output after a cursor
<example>
hub(i="…", op="logs", name="web", follow=True, cursor=1842, timeout=30)
</example>
# Drive a REPL/debugger over stdin
<example>
hub(i="…", op="send", name="debugger", text="breakpoint set --name main")
</example>
# Interrupt a process
<example>
hub(i="…", op="send", name="debugger", keys=["CTRL_C"])
</example>
# Block until a process is ready
<example>
hub(i="…", op="wait", name="web", for="ready", timeout=30)
</example>
</examples>

function.name: todo
function.description:
**Tasks: verbatim content strings, NEVER auto-generated IDs; no "task-1"/"task-N". Pass content in `task`.**

After each successful state-changing op: if nothing is `in_progress`, the earliest `pending` task (phase order) auto-promotes to `in_progress`; if several are `in_progress`, only the earliest stays. Blocked tasks NEVER auto-promote—`unblock` first. Out-of-order completion may move pointer back to an earlier phase—expected; completed tasks NEVER revert.

## Operations

|`op`|Fields|Effect|
|---|---|---|
|`init`|`list: [{phase, items: string[]}]`|Initialize full list; replaces existing|
|`init`|`items: string[]`|Flattened single-phase init|
|`start`|`task`|Mark in progress|
|`done`|`task` or `phase`|Mark completed|
|`drop`|`task` or `phase`|Mark abandoned|
|`block`|`task` or `phase`; optional `reason`|Mark blocked: awaiting external input; never auto-promotes; excluded from stop-time incomplete-todo reminder|
|`unblock`|`task` or `phase`|Blocked task → `pending`|
|`rm`|optional `task` or `phase`|Remove task/phase; omit both → clear|
|`append`|`phase`; `items: string[]`|Append tasks to phase; lazily creates phase|
|`view`|—|Read-only; echo list|

## Anatomy

- Task content: 5–10 words; what, not how; unique identifier.
- Phase name: short noun phrase (e.g. `Foundation`, `Auth`, `Verification`); unique identifier. NEVER prefix `1.`, `A)`, `Phase 1:`.

## Rules

- Mark tasks done immediately after finishing; complete phases in order.
- NEVER make a todo call the turn's only tool call. Batch with real work: `init` with first reads/edits; each `done`/`start` with next action. Solo todo turns waste a round trip.
- Waiting on something you can't act on—a user decision, another agent, external service: `block` task (optional `reason`); remains tracked but avoids stop reminder. Blocking the active task hands `in_progress` to the next `pending` task, never back to the blocked one. `unblock` when actionable. If blocker agent-actionable, `append` an unblocking task instead.
- Keep introduced `task`/`phase` strings stable.
- Lost exact task text: `view` echoes list; NEVER guess from memory.

## Create a list

- Task requires 3+ distinct steps.
- User explicitly requests one.
- User provides a set of tasks.
- New instructions arrive mid-task: capture before proceeding.

<critical>
User gives multi-step plan—phased todo, numbered/bulleted checklist, or "N bugs/items/tasks":
- MUST `init` every item as its own task before working.
- Enumerate all; NEVER summarize into fewer tasks, sample "the important ones", drop items, or track the rest from memory.
</critical>

<examples>
# Initial setup (multi-phase)
<example>
todo(i="…", op="init", list=[{"phase": "Foundation", "items": ["CUSTH-4 crate", "Wire workspace"]}, {"phase": "Auth", "items": ["Port credential store", "Wire OAuth providers"]}, {"phase": "Verification", "items": ["Run cargo test"]}])
</example>
# View current state (read-only)
<example i="…">
view
</example>
# Initial setup (single phase)
<example>
todo(i="…", op="init", list=[{"phase": "Implementation", "items": ["Apply fix", "Run tests"]}])
</example>
# Complete one task
<example>
todo(i="…", op="done", task="Wire workspace")
</example>
# Complete a whole phase
<example>
todo(i="…", op="done", phase="Auth")
</example>
# Remove all tasks
<example i="…">
rm
</example>
# Drop one task
<example>
todo(i="…", op="drop", task="Run cargo test")
</example>
# Append tasks to a phase
<example>
todo(i="…", op="append", phase="Auth", items=["Handle retries", "Run tests"])
</example>
</examples>

items.description: tasks for single-phase init or append

function.name: web_search
function.description:
Web search: current information beyond knowledge cutoff.

<instruction>
- SHOULD prefer primary sources (papers, official docs); corroborate key claims with multiple sources.
- MUST link cited sources in final response.
- NEVER use for programmatically accessible content or known URLs (GitHub repos/issues, known arXiv papers, Wikipedia pages, official docs) — `read` URL directly.
- `query`: every provider supports Google-style `site:`/`-site:`, `after:`/`before:` (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `inurl:`, `intitle:`, `filetype:`, `"exact phrase"`, `-term`, `OR`. Map constraints to native filters when available; otherwise filter results leniently. If a constraint matches nothing, relax and report it; do not return zero results.
</instruction>

function.name: write
function.description:
Creates or overwrites file at specified path.

<conditions>
- Creating new files explicitly required by task
- Replacing entire file contents when editing would be more complex
- Supports `.zip` (and ZIP-based `.jar`/`.war`/`.ear`/`.apk`), `.tar`, `.tar.gz`/`.tgz`, `.tar.zst`, and `.asar` archive entries via `archive.ext:path/inside/archive`; other archive formats (`.rar`, `.7z`, `.iso`, …) are read-only
- Supports SQLite row operations via `db.sqlite:table` (insert), `db.sqlite:table:key` (update with JSON content, delete with empty content)
</conditions>

<critical>
- You SHOULD use Edit tool for modifying existing files
- You NEVER create documentation files (*.md, README) unless explicitly requested
- You NEVER use emojis unless requested
</critical>

function.name: learn
function.description:
Capture reusable lessons in long-term memory; optionally mint/enhance a managed skill in the same call.

Use after solving insight likely to pay off again: a non-obvious fix, discovered project convention, or workflow that worked.

`skill` optional; provide only for a repeatable procedure worth codifying as `SKILL.md`, not a fact. Managed skills: isolated `~/.omp/agent/managed-skills`; surfaced as normal skills next session; NEVER touch user-authored skills. Frontmatter: generated from `name` and `description`.

Capture sparingly, specifically: one strong reusable lesson > several vague ones.

memory.description: the durable, self-contained lesson to remember (what, when, why)

context.description: optional source context for the lesson

description.description: one-line description of when to use the skill

body.description: the SKILL.md body in markdown (no frontmatter)

skill.description: also create or enhance a managed skill in the same call

function.name: manage_skill
function.description:
Managed skill: `SKILL.md` in isolated `~/.omp/agent/managed-skills`; surfaced as a normal skill in future sessions.

Use: repeatable procedures worth codifying — setup sequence, debugging recipe, project-specific workflow.
User-authored skills separate; tool NEVER edits them.

- `action: "create"` — fails if skill exists.
- `action: "update"` — overwrites body; fails if skill absent.
- `action: "delete"` — fails if skill absent.

`name`: kebab-case (lowercase letters, digits, hyphens).
`description`: specific; drives discovery.
No frontmatter in `body`; generated from `name` and `description`.

description.description: one-line description of when to use the skill (required for create/update)

body.description: the SKILL.md body in markdown, no frontmatter (required for create/update)
